To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

blobs observed in numerical simulations of a tokamak edge are due to a combination of increased parallel plasma resistivities, blob disconnection from divertor sheath potential, X-point closure, and collisional effects.

the blobs observed in the simulation are consistent with a blob dynamics model that includes the effect of increased parallel resistivity in the scrape off layer (SOL) and X-point regions, and that the blobs are disconnection events that propagate radially with E x B velocities of 1 km/s and beyond.

blobs observed in 3-D BOUT simulations are due to a combination of the following effects: (1) increased parallel plasma resistivities due to neutral cooling in the X-point, (2) the blob disconnection from divertor sheaths, (3) X-point closure of current loops, and (4) the collisionality of plasma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dynamics of plasma blobs in 3D simulations of the edge region of diverted tokamak plasmas.
the dynamics of plasma blobs in a diverted, neutral fueled tokamak edge plasma.
understanding the physics of edge plasma blobs in the presence of a magnetic separatrix and a neutral gas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
blob dynamics in the divertor region is a complex, multi-scale, multi-physics problem that can be understood by considering the interplay of the various physics processes.
the blob model is consistent with the 3D BOLT simulations and with experimental results.
blob dynamics is a consequence of the 3D nature of the edge turbulence and that blob dynamics is not the cause of 3D turbulence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 3D blob physics is consistent with the blob dynamics model and the 3D BOLT simulation results.
blobs are a natural consequence of the edge plasma turbulence, and are not an artifact of numerical instabilities or other simulation effects.
blob dynamics in 3-D is a combination of 2-D blob dynamics and the effects of magnetic topology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
blob dynamics in the scrape-off layer of a tokamak is not a purely electrostatic problem.
the observed blob dynamics can be explained by a combination of the 3D physics and the collisional physics.
blobs are not necessarily the result of an instability, but may be sustained by the plasma itself, and that the blob dynamics model is able to explain blob propagation in the divertor.
